definition: A dense vector of numbers that represents a word, sentence or object in a space where similar meanings are close together.
details: Embeddings map discrete symbols into continuous vector spaces learned from co-occurrence and context statistics. Words with similar meanings end up near each other, and directions in the space can encode relationships (such as analogies). Modern systems embed tokens inside the network and embed whole texts as a single vector for search and retrieval.
story: Imagine a chef tasting every ingredient before it goes into the pot, deciding what belongs and what would ruin the broth. Better ingredients make a better meal, and the same is true here. Every machine is shaped by what it was shown, so someone has to choose that material with care. It is the raw material; the model is only ever as good as what it was fed. That care with the raw material is Embedding.

citation.title: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality
citation.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26 (NeurIPS)

explainer.lead: An embedding turns something discrete — a word, a sentence, an image, a product — into a list of numbers placed so that similar things end up close together.
explainer.eli5: Think of a giant map where every word gets a spot. Words that mean similar things, like "cat" and "kitten", are placed next to each other, so a computer can measure meaning by measuring distance.
explainer.practitioner: Use a pretrained embedding model (e.g. a sentence-transformers model or a hosted embeddings API) to map text to fixed-length vectors, normalise them, and compare with cosine similarity. Store them in a vector index for semantic search, clustering, deduplication or RAG retrieval. Re-embed everything when you change models — vectors from different models are not comparable.
explainer.paperLevel: An embedding is a learned map f: X → ℝ^d trained so that geometric relations reflect a task signal — co-occurrence for word2vec and GloVe, contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE for sentence and image encoders (SimCSE, CLIP), or the input lookup table of a language model. Linear regularities like king − man + woman ≈ queen (Mikolov et al., 2013) emerge from factorising co-occurrence statistics.
explainer.intuition: Meaning becomes geometry: distance and direction in the vector space stand in for similarity and relationships.
howItWorks: Pick the unit to embed: tokens, sentences, documents, images or users.
Train (or reuse) a model whose objective pulls related items together and pushes unrelated ones apart.
Read the model's output or hidden layer as a fixed-length vector for each item.
Compare vectors with cosine similarity or dot product to search, cluster or classify.
explainer.example: Embedding "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login" gives vectors with high cosine similarity even though they share no words, so a support search engine can match them.
explainer.whyItMatters: Embeddings are how neural networks read discrete data at all, and they power semantic search, recommendations and the retrieval step of RAG.
misconceptions: Dimensions are not individually meaningful features; meaning lives in the overall geometry.
Embeddings inherit biases from their training data, so similarity can encode stereotypes.
